551	/// Clip ▸ Nest (⌘G) and Un-nest (⇧⌘G) — the two grouping commands
552	/// `EditorViewController.swift` forwards here (spec §4.4, §6).
553	///
554	/// Both are one op and one undo step, and every decision that could be the
555	/// core's is: which track the nest clip lands on, what span it covers, what
556	/// the nest's canvas is frozen at, where the contents come back to, and which
557	/// of the documented refusals applies. What is left on this side is the one
558	/// thing the core cannot answer — what should be SELECTED afterwards — and
559	/// the menu validation.
560	///
561	/// **Selection is read back, never predicted.** A nest replaces n clips with
562	/// one and an un-nest does the reverse, so in both cases the selection worth
563	/// having is "whatever is on the timeline now that was not there before": the
564	/// id-set difference `EditorViewController+AddClips.swift` and
565	/// `+Clipboard.swift` already use. Reading `next_id` first would work today
566	/// and would be a third place to be wrong the day the core mints ids
567	/// differently.
568	///
569	/// ## The way in is next door
570	///
571	/// The gesture this file looks like it should carry — double-click a nest
572	/// clip, the timeline and canvas show its contents, a breadcrumb leads back
573	/// out — is `EditorViewController+NestScope.swift`'s, and it exists (road map
574	/// 2's phase 9). It is worth reading what USED to be written here, because it
575	/// was true and it is what changed:
576	///
577	/// - **No op could address a clip inside a nest.** Every clip argument in the
578	///   op table resolves through `Project::clip`, which searches `self.clips`
579	///   and nothing else, and a nest's clips live in `Nest::clips`. So an inside
580	///   view could only ever have been READ-ONLY, which is worse than absent:
581	///   `TimelineView` builds its ops out of the snapshot it is handed, so every
582	///   drag, trim, split and delete would have emitted an op naming an id the
583	///   core refuses.
584	/// - What the feature needed first was a way to NAME a nested clip, and this
585	///   file said so: "an op-table decision (a path-valued `clip` argument, or a
586	///   `nest` scope on the envelope), not a new idea". It is the second of
587	///   those. `core/src/scope.rs` gives the ENVELOPE a `scope`, and the op is
588	///   applied to a view project whose top level is the nest — so
589	///   `Project::clip` kept its one meaning, no op gained a branch, and
590	///   `rc_project_scoped` hands the same view to the app to draw from.
591	///
592	/// The round trip — ⇧⌘G, edit, ⌘G — still works and is still the identity on
593	/// clip content. What it costs, and what going inside now saves, is the nest
594	/// CLIP's own transform, opacity, fades and volume: the group-level
595	/// properties, which an unnest throws away and a scope leaves alone.
596	///
597	/// Both commands here work INSIDE a nest, with no code of their own for it:
598	/// they read `document.editedProject` and their ops are stamped with the
599	/// scope by `ProjectDocument.applyEdit`, so ⌘G in a nest makes a nest in a
600	/// nest — a legal extra level, bounded by `MAX_NEST_DEPTH` on the merged
601	/// parent like any other.
602	extension EditorViewController {
603	
604	    // MARK: - Nest
605	
606	    /// ⌘G. Collapses the selection into one clip standing for the group, and
607	    /// selects it so it can be moved, faded or transformed straight away.
608	    ///
609	    /// No refusal beep of its own: `ProjectDocument.applyEdit` already beeps
610	    /// for both of the core's "nothing changed" answers — an identity (an
611	    /// empty selection, a lone nest clip) and the overlap rule's refusal of a
612	    /// nest clip that will not fit — and a second one here would double it. The only beep left is the guard below, which the menu
613	    /// validation makes unreachable from the menu but not from the key
614	    /// equivalent's own path.
615	    func nestSelection() {
616	        guard let document = document else { return }
617	        // `selectedClips` is ordered by start, so two runs over the same
618	        // selection build the same op JSON. `document.selection` is a Set and
619	        // would not.
620	        let clips = selectedClips.map { $0.id }
621	        guard !clips.isEmpty else {
622	            NSSound.beep()
623	            return
624	        }
625	        let before = document.editedProject.snapshot
626	        document.applyEdit("Nest", .nest(clips: clips))
627	        selectClips(addedSince: before, in: document)
628	    }
629	
630	    // MARK: - Un-nest
631	
632	    /// ⇧⌘G. Opens every nest clip in the selection and selects everything
633	    /// that came out of them.
634	    ///
635	    /// All of them in ONE undo step: "open this group" is one intention
636	    /// whether the user picked one nest or four, and four steps to undo it
637	    /// would be four surprises. Building every op from the same before-state
638	    /// is safe because `unnest` only ever removes the clip it names and mints
639	    /// fresh ids for the rest — no id in the list can be invalidated by an
640	    /// earlier op in it, and the tracks an earlier op inserts shift indices,
641	    /// never ids.
642	    func unnestSelection() {
643	        guard let document = document else { return }
644	        let nests = selectedClips.filter { $0.source.nestID != nil }
645	        guard !nests.isEmpty else {
646	            NSSound.beep()
647	            return
648	        }
649	        let before = document.editedProject.snapshot
650	        document.applyEdit(
651	            nests.count == 1 ? "Un-nest" : "Un-nest Clips",
652	            nests.map { ReelOp.unnest(clip: $0.id) })
653	        selectClips(addedSince: before, in: document)
654	    }
655	
656	    // MARK: - Validation
657	
658	    /// The half of `validateUserInterfaceItem` this file owns. nil means "not
659	    /// mine" and leaves the base file's answer alone.
660	    ///
661	    /// Only the CHEAP halves of the core's refusals are mirrored. Menu
662	    /// validation runs on every event pass, and the third refusal — the nest
663	    /// clip would overlap something that was NOT selected — can only be
664	    /// answered by applying the op to a throwaway project, which is what
665	    /// `EditorViewController+AddClips.swift` does once per invocation and
666	    /// nothing should do once per keystroke. A live item that beeps is the
667	    /// right trade; a menu that stutters is not.
668	    func validateNestAction(_ action: Selector) -> Bool? {
669	        switch action {
670	        case #selector(nestClips(_:)):
671	            let clips = selectedClips
672	            // The core refuses a selection of one clip that is already a
673	            // nest: wrapping a group in a group changes nothing anyone can
674	            // see. Two of them, or a nest and something else, is a real edit.
675	            if clips.count == 1, clips[0].source.nestID != nil { return false }
676	            return !clips.isEmpty
677	        case #selector(unnestClips(_:)):
678	            return selectedClips.contains { $0.source.nestID != nil }
679	        default:
680	            return nil
681	        }
682	    }
683	}

3	/// Going INSIDE a nest and coming back out — Clip ▸ Open Nest (⌘↓), Clip ▸
4	/// Close Nest (⌘↑), a double-click on a nest clip, and the breadcrumb the
5	/// timeline draws in the corner over its track headers (road map 2's phase 9,
6	/// spec §4.4).
7	///
8	/// **What made this buildable is a core change, not a view one.** Until
9	/// `core/src/scope.rs` landed, every clip argument in the op table resolved
10	/// through `Project::clip`, which searches the timeline's clips alone — so an
11	/// inside view could only ever have been read-only, and read-only would have
12	/// been worse than absent: `TimelineView` builds its ops out of the snapshot
13	/// it is handed, so every drag, trim, split and delete would have emitted an
14	/// op naming an id the core refuses. `EditorViewController+Nest.swift`'s doc
15	/// used to argue exactly that at length; it says what changed now.
16	///
17	/// What is left on this side is three things and nothing else:
18	///
19	///  - **A path, not a nest id.** The core's `scope` is one nest id, which is
20	///    all an EDIT needs. A gesture needs more: a nest can be shown by two
21	///    clips at two different starts, so the id does not say where the nest's
22	///    zero sits, and leaving has to know which container to return to and
23	///    which clip to re-select there. `ProjectDocument.nestPath` is the path,
24	///    and `NestScope` below is the arithmetic over it.
25	///  - **The playhead maps in and out.** Nest-local time is
26	///    `t − nest_clip.start` and that is the WHOLE mapping — a nest has no
27	///    speed and no in point (`core/src/nest.rs`) — so entering subtracts the
28	///    step's clip start and leaving adds it back, and the frame under the
29	///    playhead does not move.
30	///  - **Neither is an undo step.** Entering and leaving change view state
31	///    (spec §5.2's last bullet), so they register nothing, dirty nothing and
32	///    are not on ⌘Z. Leaving re-selects the nest clip, which is the clip the
33	///    person was working on before they went in.

35	/// One thing a nest clip GIVES UP for this, said out loud because it is a
36	/// removal: **a double-click on it no longer renames it.** Phase 2 put the
37	/// inline rename on `clicks == 2` (`TimelineView+Rename.swift`), and opening
38	/// a nest is the stronger meaning of that gesture in every editor that has
39	/// both. Rename is still ⇧⌘R, Clip ▸ Rename… and the Clip tab's header
40	/// field; only the shortcut moved, and only on nest clips.
41	///
42	/// The canvas shows the nest at its own frozen size with the OUTER transform
43	/// NOT applied. That is not a decision this file makes — it falls out of
44	/// `ProjectDocument.editedProject`, whose canvas IS the nest's `width`/
45	/// `height` — and it is the right one: a compound clip is edited on its own
46	/// terms, and a nest scaled to a corner of the timeline would otherwise be
47	/// edited in a postage stamp.

268	/// clips at two different starts, so without the second the playhead cannot
269	/// be mapped and leaving cannot say what to re-select.
270	struct NestScopeStep: Equatable {
271	    let nest: UInt32
272	    let clip: UInt32
273	}

275	/// Reading a `nestPath` against a project — pure functions over a snapshot,
276	/// with no document and no view in them, so `ProjectDocument.clampViewState`
277	/// and the editor can ask the same questions and get the same answers.
278	///
279	/// Every walk starts at the timeline and descends one container at a time.
280	/// `ProjectSnapshot.nests` carries each nest's own clips (they live in the
281	/// parent's one id space, spec §5.2), so the whole walk is available from the
282	/// PARENT snapshot alone — no scoped handle is built to answer any of this,
283	/// which matters because `clamped` runs on every edit, undo and redo.
284	enum NestScope {
285	    /// The clips of the container `path` opens INTO — the timeline's for an
286	    /// empty path, else the innermost nest's.
287	    static func clips(in path: [NestScopeStep], of snapshot: ProjectSnapshot) -> [ClipSnapshot] {
288	        guard let step = path.last else { return snapshot.clips }
289	        return snapshot.nest(step.nest)?.clips ?? []
290	    }
291	
292	    /// The valid prefix of `path`: every step whose nest still exists and
293	    /// whose nest clip is still in the container above it, still showing that
294	    /// nest.
295	    ///
296	    /// Truncation rather than clearing, so an undo that removes an inner nest
297	    /// leaves the person in the outer one they were also in, rather than
298	    /// throwing them out to the timeline from three levels down.
299	    static func clamped(_ path: [NestScopeStep], in snapshot: ProjectSnapshot)
300	        -> [NestScopeStep]
301	    {
302	        var kept: [NestScopeStep] = []
303	        for step in path {
304	            guard snapshot.nest(step.nest) != nil,
305	                let clip = clips(in: kept, of: snapshot).first(where: { $0.id == step.clip }),
306	                clip.source.nestID == step.nest
307	            else { break }
308	            kept.append(step)
309	        }
310	        return kept
311	    }
312	
313	    /// Where the innermost container's zero sits in PROJECT time: the sum of
314	    /// every step's nest clip start, each measured in its own container.
315	    ///
316	    /// The whole mapping, because a nest clip has no in point and a nest has
317	    /// no speed (`core/src/nest.rs`). Stops at the first step it cannot
318	    /// resolve, which `clamped` has already made unreachable on the paths the
319	    /// app holds.
320	    static func offset(of path: [NestScopeStep], in snapshot: ProjectSnapshot) -> Ticks {
321	        var total: Ticks = 0
322	        var walked: [NestScopeStep] = []
323	        for step in path {
324	            guard let clip = clips(in: walked, of: snapshot).first(where: { $0.id == step.clip })
325	            else { break }
326	            total += clip.start
327	            walked.append(step)
328	        }
329	        return total
330	    }
331	
332	    /// "Timeline", then one name per level.
333	    ///
334	    /// A level's name is the CLIP's (`ProjectSnapshot.name(of:)`, which falls
335	    /// back to the nest's own name and then to the kind), not the nest's,
336	    /// because a renamed nest clip is what the person sees on the bar they
337	    /// double-clicked. A step whose clip cannot be found still contributes a
338	    /// component, so the trail never comes out shorter than the path it is
339	    /// describing.
340	    static func names(of path: [NestScopeStep], in snapshot: ProjectSnapshot) -> [String] {
341	        var out = ["Timeline"]
342	        var walked: [NestScopeStep] = []
343	        for step in path {
344	            let clip = clips(in: walked, of: snapshot).first { $0.id == step.clip }
345	            out.append(clip.map { snapshot.name(of: $0) } ?? snapshot.nest(step.nest)?.name ?? "Nest")
346	            walked.append(step)
347	        }
348	        return out
349	    }
350	}

353	/// The nest-scope breadcrumb: the trail drawn in the corner where the track
354	/// header column and the ruler cross, and the click that walks back out of a
355	/// nest (road map 2's phase 9; the gestures and the path arithmetic are
356	/// `EditorViewController+NestScope.swift`'s).
357	///
358	/// The split is `TimelineView+Candidates.swift`'s exactly, for the same
359	/// reason: `TimelineRulerView.draw` opens by filling its whole bounds
360	/// opaquely and then paints the corner LAST, over the ticks that would
361	/// otherwise slide under the header column, so anything in that square has to
362	/// be drawn from inside that method. `TimelineView.swift` keeps one stored
363	/// property, one closure, one draw call, one hit-test token and one gesture
364	/// case; every body is here.
365	///
366	/// **The corner had to grow a hit case rather than a flag.** The frozen file's
367	/// `hit(at:)` answered `.corner` for the whole square and `beginGesture` did
368	/// `case .none, .corner: break` — the click was swallowed twice, deliberately,
369	/// because an inert square should not start a scrub. A second case keeps that
370	/// sentence exactly true at the top level and gives the square a meaning only
371	/// while there is somewhere to go.
372	///
373	/// ## What fits in 131 × 21 points
374	///
375	/// The corner is `DS.trackHeaderWidth` (132) by `DS.rulerHeight` (22), less a
376	/// one-point border down its right edge and one along the ruler's bottom. One
377	/// short level fits comfortably; two do not, and three never will. So the
378	/// trail draws its **last two components** — the container you would return
379	/// to and the one you are in — middle-truncated, with the whole path as the
380	/// tooltip. Middle truncation rather than tail, because two nests called
381	/// "Lower Third 1" and "Lower Third 2" differ at the END and a tail ellipsis
382	/// would render them identical.
383	///
384	/// **The whole cell is one target and it means "out one level"** — the same
385	/// command as ⌘↑ and as Clip ▸ Close Nest. Splitting 131 points into two
386	/// click regions so the left component could jump out several levels at once
387	/// was considered and refused: the regions would be under 60 points wide,
388	/// their boundary would move with the text, and the same journey is two
389	/// presses of a key that is already bound. The hit case carries the level all
390	/// the same (`level: Int`, counted as `ProjectDocument.nestPath` counts, 0
391	/// being the timeline), so a later design can widen the meaning without
392	/// touching the frozen file again.
393	///
394	/// ## The corner is the RULER's, so the ruler floats above the headers
395	///
396	/// The two floating bands are pinned to different edges — the ruler to the
397	/// top of the visible rectangle, the header column to its left — and they
398	/// overlap in exactly one square, this corner, and only once the pane has
399	/// been scrolled VERTICALLY: at rest the header column begins at the ruler's
400	/// own height and the two never meet. The frozen file's `init` therefore adds
401	/// the headers FIRST and the ruler second, and that order is load-bearing.
402	/// The other way round, `TimelineHeaderView.draw`'s opening `bounds.fill()`
403	/// painted the corner out the moment the pane scrolled by a point: the
404	/// breadcrumb was invisible exactly where the way out of a nest is supposed
405	/// to be, while `cornerHit` went on answering `.breadcrumb` there — a live
406	/// click target under what drew as a track header.
407	///
408	/// Measured rather than reasoned, because it is a z-order change in a file
409	/// that had been drawing correctly for eight phases. Offscreen, a bare
410	/// `TimelineView` is rendered with a two-level trail set, at rest and
411	/// scrolled (`tools/proof/phase9_chrome.py`, over ten text tracks — 490 pt
412	/// of content against a 324 pt viewport, so its 62 pt scroll is one the app
413	/// can reach): with the headers on top the scrolled corner came out
414	/// BYTE-IDENTICAL to the same corner with no trail at all, and with the ruler
415	/// on top it comes out byte-identical to the corner AT REST — which is also
416	/// what says the swap moves nothing else, since at rest the two bands do not
417	/// meet and every render the offscreen harness makes is at rest. The
418	/// six-track probe this was first measured with OVER-SCROLLED — its 306 pt
419	/// of content was shorter than the pane, and `NSClipView.scroll(to:)` does
420	/// not clamp — while its z-order pictures held; the tracked script's
421	/// `init-order` mutant is what gates the claim now.
422	///
423	/// **What the swap does move is an open rename field**, which is a real
424	/// subview of the band it edits, and a track's field sits at its ROW's top —
425	/// so on the top, partly scrolled row it lands in this square. `beginRename`
426	/// answers that by raising whichever band holds the field to the front for
427	/// as long as it is open, and `endRename` puts the ruler back. It is
428	/// deliberately unconditional: "raise it only when the field would actually
429	/// be covered" is a geometric test taken once, at open time, that the next
430	/// scroll makes false, while "the band being typed into is the front-most
431	/// band" has no geometry in it and cannot rot. What that costs is the
432	/// breadcrumb while a track name is being typed — which is the corner this
433	/// app drew for eight phases — and the offscreen render of a field open on
434	/// that row is byte-identical before and after the swap, which is the point.
435	///
436	/// ## One gesture, one level
437	///
438	/// The frozen file's `.breadcrumb` case acts on the FIRST press only
439	/// (`clicks < 2`), and that guard is load-bearing rather than tidy. AppKit
440	/// delivers a double-click as two mouse-downs — clickCount 1, then 2 — and
441	/// this cell is not a scrub or a selection a second press can merely repeat:
442	/// it is a BUTTON that has already acted. By the time the second down
443	/// arrives the trail is one component shorter, `cornerHit` reads the NEW
444	/// trail and answers a new level, so the pair walked out TWO nests for one
445	/// gesture — inconsistently at that, since from one level down the second
446	/// press landed on a corner that had gone inert and did nothing at all. A
447	/// deliberate journey of several levels is several separate clicks, or two
448	/// presses of ⌘↑, which is the key this cell duplicates.
449	extension TimelineView {
450	    /// What a click in the corner means: nothing at the top level, and one
451	    /// level out while a nest is open.
452	    ///
453	    /// Read by `TimelineContentView.hit(at:)`, which is the one line of this
454	    /// the frozen file carries.
455	    var cornerHit: TimelineHit {
456	        guard breadcrumb.count > 1 else { return .corner }
457	        return .breadcrumb(level: breadcrumb.count - 2)
458	    }
459	
460	    /// Registers (or clears) the tooltip that carries the FULL path, since
461	    /// the drawn trail is two components and middle-truncated at that.
462	    ///
463	    /// It is a rect tooltip on the CONTENT view rather than a `toolTip` on
464	    /// the ruler, and both halves of that matter. The ruler refuses hits
465	    /// (`hitTest` answers nil unless a real subview is under the point) so
466	    /// that `TimelineContentView` can own every mouse event in the pane; and
467	    /// a whole-view `toolTip` would pop up over the ruler's entire width,
468	    /// where what has a tooltip is one 132-point square. The rect is in
469	    /// content coordinates and so moves with the scroll, which is why
470	    /// `pinFloatingBands` calls this as well as the `didSet` above.
471	    ///
472	    /// `removeAllToolTips()` is safe here for the reason app/CLAUDE.md's
473	    /// tracking-area rule makes it unsafe elsewhere: the blanket form is
474	    /// wrong when it takes `NSToolTipManager`'s areas out from under a view
475	    /// that has OTHER tooltips, and the timeline's content view has none —
476	    /// this is its only one, added and removed together.
477	    func syncBreadcrumbTooltip() {
478	        content.removeAllToolTips()
479	        guard breadcrumb.count > 1 else { return }
480	        let corner = NSRect(
481	            x: pinnedX, y: pinnedY, width: TimelineLayout.headerWidth,
482	            height: TimelineLayout.rulerHeight)
483	        _ = content.addToolTip(
484	            corner, owner: breadcrumb.joined(separator: " › ") as NSString, userData: nil)
485	    }
486	}

490	extension TimelineRulerView {
491	    /// Called from `draw(_:)` after the corner's own opaque fill and its two
492	    /// border strokes, and before the playhead's head — so the trail sits ON
493	    /// the corner and the playhead still crosses everything.
494	    ///
495	    /// Draws nothing at the top level, which is what leaves the shipped
496	    /// corner byte for byte what it was for every project that never enters a
497	    /// nest.
498	    func drawBreadcrumb(owner: TimelineView, in corner: NSRect) {
499	        let trail = owner.breadcrumb
500	        guard trail.count > 1 else { return }
501	
502	        // The last two components. `count > 1` is guaranteed above, so this
503	        // is always exactly two.
504	        let parent = trail[trail.count - 2]
505	        let here = trail[trail.count - 1]
506	
507	        // A back chevron at the left edge says the cell is a way OUT before a
508	        // word of it is read, which is the whole job of the first glance.
509	        let chevronX = corner.minX + 5
510	        let midY = corner.midY - 1
511	        let chevron = NSBezierPath()
512	        chevron.move(to: NSPoint(x: chevronX + 3.5, y: midY - 3.5))
513	        chevron.line(to: NSPoint(x: chevronX, y: midY))
514	        chevron.line(to: NSPoint(x: chevronX + 3.5, y: midY + 3.5))
515	        chevron.lineWidth = 1.5
516	        chevron.lineCapStyle = .round
517	        chevron.lineJoinStyle = .round
518	        DS.textMuted.setStroke()
519	        chevron.stroke()
520	
521	        // Inside the corner's right-hand border, past the chevron.
522	        let box = NSRect(
523	            x: chevronX + 8, y: 3, width: max(corner.maxX - 3 - (chevronX + 8), 0),
524	            height: corner.height - 5)
525	        guard box.width > 8 else { return }
526	
527	        // The parent muted and the current level strong: the pair reads as
528	        // "where you came from › where you are" without a legend. Middle
529	        // truncation, not tail, because two nests called "Lower Third 1" and
530	        // "Lower Third 2" differ at the END.
531	        let style = NSMutableParagraphStyle()
532	        style.lineBreakMode = .byTruncatingMiddle
533	        let muted: [NSAttributedString.Key: Any] = [
534	            .font: DS.sans(10), .foregroundColor: DS.textMuted, .paragraphStyle: style,
535	        ]
536	        let strong: [NSAttributedString.Key: Any] = [
537	            .font: DS.sans(10, weight: .semibold), .foregroundColor: DS.textStrong,
538	            .paragraphStyle: style,
539	        ]
540	        let line = NSMutableAttributedString(string: parent, attributes: muted)
541	        line.append(NSAttributedString(string: " › ", attributes: muted))
542	        line.append(NSAttributedString(string: here, attributes: strong))
543	        NSGraphicsContext.current?.saveGraphicsState()
544	        NSBezierPath(rect: box).addClip()
545	        line.draw(with: box, options: [.usesLineFragmentOrigin, .truncatesLastVisibleLine])
546	        NSGraphicsContext.current?.restoreGraphicsState()
547	    }
548	}

551	/// Clip ▸ Nest (⌘G) and Un-nest (⇧⌘G) — the two grouping commands
552	/// `EditorViewController.swift` forwards here (spec §4.4, §6).
553	///
554	/// Both are one op and one undo step, and every decision that could be the
555	/// core's is: which track the nest clip lands on, what span it covers, what
556	/// the nest's canvas is frozen at, where the contents come back to, and which
557	/// of the documented refusals applies. What is left on this side is the one
558	/// thing the core cannot answer — what should be SELECTED afterwards — and
559	/// the menu validation.
560	///
561	/// **Selection is read back, never predicted.** A nest replaces n clips with
562	/// one and an un-nest does the reverse, so in both cases the selection worth
563	/// having is "whatever is on the timeline now that was not there before": the
564	/// id-set difference `EditorViewController+AddClips.swift` and
565	/// `+Clipboard.swift` already use. Reading `next_id` first would work today
566	/// and would be a third place to be wrong the day the core mints ids
567	/// differently.
568	///
569	/// ## The way in is next door
570	///
571	/// The gesture this file looks like it should carry — double-click a nest
572	/// clip, the timeline and canvas show its contents, a breadcrumb leads back
573	/// out — is `EditorViewController+NestScope.swift`'s, and it exists (road map
574	/// 2's phase 9). It is worth reading what USED to be written here, because it
575	/// was true and it is what changed:
576	///
577	/// - **No op could address a clip inside a nest.** Every clip argument in the
578	///   op table resolves through `Project::clip`, which searches `self.clips`
579	///   and nothing else, and a nest's clips live in `Nest::clips`. So an inside
580	///   view could only ever have been READ-ONLY, which is worse than absent:
581	///   `TimelineView` builds its ops out of the snapshot it is handed, so every
582	///   drag, trim, split and delete would have emitted an op naming an id the
583	///   core refuses.
584	/// - What the feature needed first was a way to NAME a nested clip, and this
585	///   file said so: "an op-table decision (a path-valued `clip` argument, or a
586	///   `nest` scope on the envelope), not a new idea". It is the second of
587	///   those. `core/src/scope.rs` gives the ENVELOPE a `scope`, and the op is
588	///   applied to a view project whose top level is the nest — so
589	///   `Project::clip` kept its one meaning, no op gained a branch, and
590	///   `rc_project_scoped` hands the same view to the app to draw from.
591	///
592	/// The round trip — ⇧⌘G, edit, ⌘G — still works and is still the identity on
593	/// clip content. What it costs, and what going inside now saves, is the nest
594	/// CLIP's own transform, opacity, fades and volume: the group-level
595	/// properties, which an unnest throws away and a scope leaves alone.
596	///
597	/// Both commands here work INSIDE a nest, with no code of their own for it:
598	/// they read `document.editedProject` and their ops are stamped with the
599	/// scope by `ProjectDocument.applyEdit`, so ⌘G in a nest makes a nest in a
600	/// nest — a legal extra level, bounded by `MAX_NEST_DEPTH` on the merged
601	/// parent like any other.
602	extension EditorViewController {
603	
604	    // MARK: - Nest
605	
606	    /// ⌘G. Collapses the selection into one clip standing for the group, and
607	    /// selects it so it can be moved, faded or transformed straight away.
608	    ///
609	    /// No refusal beep of its own: `ProjectDocument.applyEdit` already beeps
610	    /// for both of the core's "nothing changed" answers — an identity (an
611	    /// empty selection, a lone nest clip) and the overlap rule's refusal of a
612	    /// nest clip that will not fit — and a second one here would double it. The only beep left is the guard below, which the menu
613	    /// validation makes unreachable from the menu but not from the key
614	    /// equivalent's own path.
615	    func nestSelection() {
616	        guard let document = document else { return }
617	        // `selectedClips` is ordered by start, so two runs over the same
618	        // selection build the same op JSON. `document.selection` is a Set and
619	        // would not.
620	        let clips = selectedClips.map { $0.id }
621	        guard !clips.isEmpty else {
622	            NSSound.beep()
623	            return
624	        }
625	        let before = document.editedProject.snapshot
626	        document.applyEdit("Nest", .nest(clips: clips))
627	        selectClips(addedSince: before, in: document)
628	    }
629	
630	    // MARK: - Un-nest
631	
632	    /// ⇧⌘G. Opens every nest clip in the selection and selects everything
633	    /// that came out of them.
634	    ///
635	    /// All of them in ONE undo step: "open this group" is one intention
636	    /// whether the user picked one nest or four, and four steps to undo it
637	    /// would be four surprises. Building every op from the same before-state
638	    /// is safe because `unnest` only ever removes the clip it names and mints
639	    /// fresh ids for the rest — no id in the list can be invalidated by an
640	    /// earlier op in it, and the tracks an earlier op inserts shift indices,
641	    /// never ids.
642	    func unnestSelection() {
643	        guard let document = document else { return }
644	        let nests = selectedClips.filter { $0.source.nestID != nil }
645	        guard !nests.isEmpty else {
646	            NSSound.beep()
647	            return
648	        }
649	        let before = document.editedProject.snapshot
650	        document.applyEdit(
651	            nests.count == 1 ? "Un-nest" : "Un-nest Clips",
652	            nests.map { ReelOp.unnest(clip: $0.id) })
653	        selectClips(addedSince: before, in: document)
654	    }
655	
656	    // MARK: - Validation
657	
658	    /// The half of `validateUserInterfaceItem` this file owns. nil means "not
659	    /// mine" and leaves the base file's answer alone.
660	    ///
661	    /// Only the CHEAP halves of the core's refusals are mirrored. Menu
662	    /// validation runs on every event pass, and the third refusal — the nest
663	    /// clip would overlap something that was NOT selected — can only be
664	    /// answered by applying the op to a throwaway project, which is what
665	    /// `EditorViewController+AddClips.swift` does once per invocation and
666	    /// nothing should do once per keystroke. A live item that beeps is the
667	    /// right trade; a menu that stutters is not.
668	    func validateNestAction(_ action: Selector) -> Bool? {
669	        switch action {
670	        case #selector(nestClips(_:)):
671	            let clips = selectedClips
672	            // The core refuses a selection of one clip that is already a
673	            // nest: wrapping a group in a group changes nothing anyone can
674	            // see. Two of them, or a nest and something else, is a real edit.
675	            if clips.count == 1, clips[0].source.nestID != nil { return false }
676	            return !clips.isEmpty
677	        case #selector(unnestClips(_:)):
678	            return selectedClips.contains { $0.source.nestID != nil }
679	        default:
680	            return nil
681	        }
682	    }
683	}

# app/CLAUDE.md — Swift app rules

Applies to everything under `app/`. Build/verification commands and the FFI
lockstep are in the root `CLAUDE.md`; the full design is
`designs/spec/` (§3–4 the UI, §7.4–7.8 the platform side; its `README.md` is
the index). The
long form of each entry below — why each file is the shape it is, and the
traps its history turned up — is `designs/adr/app-file-history.md` (the
full history, every size toll and measurement, is archived; see its
"Original" line); this file is what governs a file now. Files
are listed by family; a file with a header comment of its own carries its
detail there.

## File map

**The core's edge.**
- `ReelCore.swift` — with its `ReelCore+<Area>.swift` files, the only files
  that call `rc_*` (spec §11 CJ-8 (l)); a new wrapper goes in the file of its
  area. `ReelCore.swift` holds `ReelProject`
  (handle + lazily decoded `ProjectSnapshot`; `json`, `snapshot` and
  `planJSON` are memoised PER HANDLE, so keep handles rather than minting
  them; so is `sourceMap(_:)`, `rc_project_source_map` decoded and checked
  once per handle and clip, SR-20), timecode, snapping (export presets/sizes/settings are
  `ExportValues.swift`'s, a pure move, HDR H-1), `ReelSpeed.limits` (the
  core's speed range and audio ceiling, typed as `SpeedLimits` in
  `CoreValues.swift` — no Swift file types a speed bound), `ReelColor` (`rc_normalise_color`, G-25) and `ReelAgentSocket` (below);
  `ReelCore+MediaFiles.swift` holds the media files the core reads or writes —
  `ReelContainer` (`rc_container_*`, a WebM/Matroska file's index, #216-R), `ReelCube`,
  `ReelHDR10` (`rc_hdr10_peak`, spec §11 HD-6; `av1Peak`, `rc_hdr10_av1_peak`, HD-18;
  `stillPeak`, `rc_hdr10_still_peak`, HD-20), `ReelAV1` and `ReelWebM` (`rc_webm_*`, the
  `av1_webm` writer, spec §11 CX-15) — `ReelCore+Cursor.swift` holds `ReelCursor`
  (`rc_cursor_open`, `rc_cursor_free`: a cursor file's open, which is its check, spec
  §11 CU-9, CU-15; road map creator-jobs CU1a; and `query`, `rc_cursor_query`'s one
  JSON request, CU2, spec §11 CU-25, and the static `query(_:tracks:project:)`, the
  same call over n tracks with a project (`plan_zooms`, CU-70)) — `ReelCore+Framing.swift`
  holds `SpeakerMatch` and `ReelProject.speakerMatch` (`rc_project_speaker_match`, road map
  creator-jobs VR6b, spec §11 VR-65: the face-to-microphone match Make Vertical's sheet
  confirms) — and `ReelCore+Graphics.swift` the graphics engine's
  wrappers (below), with `ReelGraphicPackage` (`rc_graphic_package_write`, G-46; `read`,
  `rc_graphic_package_read`, G-47), `GraphicLibrary.usage()` (`rc_graphic_library_usage`)
  and `GraphicLibrary.imageCache(limit:)` (`rc_graphic_image_cache`, G-39) — both pure moves
  out of `ReelCore.swift` (road map creator-jobs CJ0d, T15); `ReelCoreError`, `Fps.ffiPair` and `ReelTime`'s
  seconds conversions are `CoreValues.swift`'s (G6 phase 5's toll T2 and speed ramps SR4-0,
  pure moves); the typed patches are `TypedPatches.swift`'s (`VideoPatch`,
  `AudioPatch`, `ClipPatch`, the `ActionPatch` extension; a pure move, B73),
  `TextPatch` (with `case`, `words` and `word_style`) is `TextPatch.swift`'s,
  moved out so it could grow, and `ShapePatch` `ShapePatch.swift`'s (a pure
  move, the toll for `ReelColor`). `VideoPatch.color` is a sparse `ColorPatch`
  (`GradeProps.swift`, which holds `ColorAdjust` (moved out of
  `ProjectSnapshot.swift`, grading-2 G2-0) with its neutrality helpers, and
  `LayerUniforms.apply(tone:)`, and the wheels' `ColorWheel`, `ColorWheels`,
  `ColorWheelPatch`, `ColorWheelsPatch`, `ColorWheelKind` and
  `LayerUniforms.apply(wheels:)` (GR-11)); `VideoPatch.curves` is
  `CurveProps.swift`'s `ColorCurvesPatch`, beside `CurvePoint`,
  `CurveDomain`, `CurveChannel`, `CurveBlend` (a channel blended inside an
  action, spec §11 GR-34; `ColorCurves.blends`, never encoded), `ColorCurves` and
  `LayerUniforms.apply(curves:)` (GR-12, the hue curves GR-32; a
  pure move out of `GradeProps.swift`, grading-4 T4-0); `VideoPatch.qualifier` is
  `QualifierProps.swift`'s `ColorQualifierPatch`, beside `ColorQualifier` (its
  `blur`, `blursSelection` and `selectionSigma`, GR-35), `QualifierUniforms`
  (`blurred`, set only by `drawAdjustment`) and the pick's `QualifierSample`
  (GR-13), so a row writes
  only its own key to every selected clip. `word_style` has ONE
  app-side writer, `CaptionLayout.place` (W-10). `ReelAgentSocket` (road map
  14's MC2) wraps `rc_agent_socket_start` / `_release`: `start` throws the
  core's sentence, `release` is the quit's unlink-if-still-ours with no join;
  `answer(_:)` hands the tool callback's answer back through
  `rc_agent_string_create` (CJ0d's T15c), a plain static because the trampoline
  runs on the core's server thread, so `AgentServer.swift` names no `rc_*`.
  The `dictionary` extensions on the property types are
  `OpDictionaries.swift`'s (below).
  The graphics engine's wrappers are `ReelCore+Graphics.swift`'s: `GraphicLibrary` (`addFont`,
  `addAsset`, `rasterize`, `families()`; frozen by its first compile,
  rasterize or `families()`) and
  `GraphicModule` (`compile`, `describeJSON`, `svg`; it holds its library
  strongly); their values `GraphicDiagnostic` (with `.error`, `.noModule`
  and `.of(_:)`, the one spelling of a diagnostic made from a message, a
  missing module or a thrown error), `GraphicFailure` (what a
  `diag_out` failure throws; `err_out` stays `ReelCoreError`) and
  `GraphicRaster` are `CoreValues.swift`'s, with `GraphicUsage`, the byte
  bridges `withByteBuffer` and `withMutableByteBuffer` (G-46's toll; never
  `UnsafeMutablePointer(mutating:)`), `SpeedLimits` (a pure move,
  clean-up batch 2), `ReelCoreError` and `Fps.ffiPair` (G6 phase 5's toll), and
  `CoreJSON` (`value`, `snapTicks`: `clipState`'s and `snapCandidates`' JSON
  halves, clean-up round 3's toll; `array`, `overrides`, C1's tolls; `ExportSize.list`,
  `ExportSettings.decoded`, `ReelAV1.Config.decoded`, `withNonNullBytes`, codec-export C5's
  toll), and C1's
  fix-pass moves: `ReelAV1.Config` / `.Color` (an extension of
  `ReelCore+MediaFiles.swift`'s `ReelAV1`, whose `rc_av1_*` calls stay there), `GraphicDiagnostic.list(json:)`,
  `GraphicFailure.checkSides`, `SpeedLimits.decoded` and the free `withBytes`.
  `MediaDescriptor`, `MediaOriginal`, `mediaURL(for:)`, `originalURL(for:)`,
  `revealURL(for:)` (the original, else the copy), `cursorURL(for:)` (the
  cursor file: its bookmark when it resolves, else the stored path, existing or
  not), `isTrashed` and
  `bookmarkString(for:)` are `MediaDescriptor.swift`'s: a `media[]` element
  minus its id, and the media-file resolvers; they call no `rc_*`.
  It is also where the op table is read BACK: `ReelOp.coreNames()` over
  `rc_op_names`, and `ReelOp.coreSchemas()` over `rc_op_schemas` — every
  op's ARGUMENTS as JSON Schema, keyed by op name, which
  `AgentCatalog.opTool` prints for all sixty-nine op tools.
  `deinit` frees the Rust allocation. It also holds **the one read of
  `rc_project_apply`'s TWO message channels**, in the header's own order — a
  sentence is a refusal, an error message is invalid input, neither written
  is an identity — answered as the `ReelEdit` below.
- `OpDictionaries.swift` — the `dictionary` extensions on the §5.2
  property types (`CropInsets` … `Gradient`), the model's own key names; a
  pure move out of `ReelCore.swift` (#190, issue batch B52b; road map 14's
  MC2 made the same move as `PropsDictionaries.swift`, and the merge kept
  main's file). With
  `ReelCore.swift` and `ReelOps.swift`, the only files that write an op
  argument. `putNullable` is the one writer of a three-state (`T??`)
  patch key: absent, an explicit null, or the value.
- `ReelOps.swift` — `OpArgs`, `ReelOp` and one typed factory per row of
  `core/src/edit.rs`'s op table, plus a RAW factory beside the typed one at
  each door that takes a CALLER's own object — ELEVEN of them (`setVideoRaw`,
  `setAudioRaw`, `setTextRaw`, `setShapeRaw`, `setClipRaw`,
  `setActionEndRaw`, `addTextClipRaw`, `addShapeClipRaw`, `setCanvasRaw`,
  `addBackgroundRaw`, `addZoomActionRaw`), which takes the
  caller's own object as `Any` — never `[String: Any]`, so a non-object is
  refused by the CORE in the words that name the group — and forwards it;
  there is no untyped op-JSON call site anywhere else. Where only ONE
  argument is the caller's (a colour, a region, a new clip's patch) the typed
  factory DELEGATES to the raw one, mapping its optional explicitly, because
  an `Optional<T>.none` widened to `Any?` is a non-nil `Any` wrapping a nil.
  The typed `setActionEnd` LIFTS every top-level null out of its patch into
  `off` (spec §11 CI-14: a typed `.some(nil)` is a switch turned OFF, kept
  at the end), and a null slot inside `audio.eq` into `audio.eq.<slot>`
  (AU-88); `setActionEndRaw`'s nulls stay removals, which is what
  `clearOps` and every agent call send, and it writes `off` only when non-empty and `schema` only when non-nil
  (the agent door fills it for a graphic end from the module's current
  revision, spec §11 G-34).
  `addZoomActionRaw`'s region is `Any` and not `Any?`: an absent key and an
  explicit null are opposite intentions there, and only the tool can tell
  them apart.
  `scope` is a member folded into `json`; `documentLevelNames` MIRRORS
  `scope.rs`'s `refused_inside` (eleven names: its twelve arms but
  `add_adjustment_clip`, sent scoped) so one edit can mix a
  document-level op with scoped ones. A table, with
  `edit.rs`'s size exemption.
- `ReelOpSchema.swift` — what an op TAKES, mirroring what
  `core/src/op_schema.rs` publishes: the `properties` and `required` of one
  op's arguments, which are the two things `AgentServer.tool` takes, and
  `table(from:)`, which reads `rc_op_schemas`' JSON into them (SR4-0's pure
  move out of `ReelCore.swift`, whose `coreSchemas()` keeps the call). Here
  rather than next door for `ReelEdit.swift`'s reason — it names no `rc_*`
  symbol — and `properties` stays `[String: Any]` because a Swift type per
  kind would be another spelling of the table.
- `ReelEdit.swift` — what an op ANSWERS, mirroring `core/src/outcome.rs`:
  `ReelEdit` (`.applied` / `.identity` / `.refused`), `ReelRefusal` (the op
  the core declined and the rule's own sentence, carried verbatim), and the
  fold that applies a LIST — which names no `rc_*` symbol, so it lives here
  and not next door. **Only `.applied` is an undo step**; the other two are
  both "the project did not change" and differ only in what a caller can
  SAY. `.project` is the spelling for a caller that treats a refusal as
  nothing happened (a probe, a live drag), and there is one on
  `ReelEdit?` too for the `try?` probes. In the fold **a refusal does not
  stop the list** — a later op still runs after one, exactly as after an
  identity — and the FIRST refusal is answered only when nothing applied.
- `ProjectSnapshot.swift` · `VideoProps.swift` · `ClipSnapshot.swift` ·
  `TrackSnapshot.swift` · `TextProps.swift` · `MotionProps.swift` ·
  `WordProps.swift` · `MediaSnapshot.swift` · `ActionSnapshot.swift` · `ShapeProps.swift` · `CompositionPlan.swift` · `GradeProps.swift` · `CurveProps.swift` · `AudioProps.swift` · `CursorProps.swift` · `CutoutProps.swift` — the `Codable`, READ-ONLY mirror
  of spec §5.2 every view draws from. READ-ONLY means never written back as
  is: the stored properties are `var`, so a writer edits a COPY
  (`var s = current(); s.blur = v`) rather than rebuilding one through the
  defaulted memberwise initialiser, which silently drops a field it does not
  spell out; `MotionProps.with(_:)` is motion's per-slot copy (#357). `CompositionPlan.swift` (a pure move out of
  `ProjectSnapshot.swift`, grading GR1) is the plan's Swift side (spec §7.2): `PlanSegment`,
  `PlanRamp`, `PlanTrack`, `PlanInstruction` and `CompositionPlan`; `PlanSpeedRamp.source` is
  its `map` as a `SourceMap`, checked once at decode and not a coding key (SR-20 (c));
  `PlanSegment.path` (the clip alone when absent) and `origin` (nil) read a nested audio
  segment's instance (spec §11 TX-10); `PlanDuck`
  and `ducks` are a speech ducker's own multiplier (format 29, spec §11 AU-113); `PlanGate` and
  `gates` a gated clip's hide-while-silent gate (format 43, spec §11 CO-93). `AudioProps.swift`
  (a pure move out of `ProjectSnapshot.swift`, road map "audio" AP11's toll) holds the audio group:
  `AudioProps`, `DuckProps` and `CompressorProps`, with format 29's `DuckMode`,
  `DuckProps.mode` / `preRoll` / `hold` and `FadeShape` (and the popups' titles), and format
  30's `LimiterProps` (`audio.limiter`, spec §11 AU-21) with its patch body,
  and format 31's `AudioProps.isolation` (AU-50), and format 32's `eq`, `hum` and `channels`
  (`AudioEQProps.swift`, AU-31, AU-33, AU-34), and format 33's `gate` and `deEsser`
  (`AudioDynamicsProps.swift`, AU-43, AU-45), and format 34's `voice`
  (`VoiceProps.swift`, AU-140), and format 37's `leveller`
  (`AudioDynamicsProps.swift`, AU-66);
  `ClipSnapshot.swift`'s `TransitionSnapshot.audioShape` is `plus_3db` when absent, and
  `MediaSnapshot.speech` the media's saved spans. `CursorProps.swift` (format 38, road map
  creator-jobs CU3a1, spec §11 CU-30, CU-39) holds `CursorStyle`, `CursorClicks` (`off` is the
  core's `none`: a case named `none` warns), `CursorProps` (`VideoProps.cursor` and
  `VideoPatch.cursor`; its `dictionary` writes all eight keys, `NSNull` for a nil `hideIdle`),
  `CursorPatch` (all eight keys, the sparse write `VideoPatch.cursorPart` carries — written
  under `cursor` only when `cursor` is nil, never decoded, `cutoutPart`'s shape — so each Cursor
  row writes its own key alone, CU3b, CU4, spec §11 CU-38 (b), CU-40; `clipsOwn` (smoothing,
  hide_idle) and `animatable` (the other six)), with `CursorProps.smoothingSteps`,
  `hideIdleSteps` and `polished`,
  `MediaCursor` (`MediaSnapshot.cursor`, `MediaDescriptor.cursor`, kept by `probeDictionary`) and
  `RecipeCursor` (the recipe layer's `cursor`, `media` and `at` required).
  `CutoutProps.swift` (format 39, road map creator-jobs CO2a1, spec §11 CO-20, CO-21;
  `foreground` and the image arm format 41, CO10a, CO-100, CO-101) holds `CutoutSubject`
  (`person`, `foreground`), `CutoutQuality`, `CutoutBackground`, `CutoutProps` (`VideoProps.cutout` and
  `VideoPatch.cutout`; its `dictionary` writes all five keys), `CutoutPatch` (the sparse
  write `VideoPatch.cutoutPart` carries — written under `cutout` only when `cutout` is nil,
  never decoded — so a Background, Edge or Feather row writes its own key alone, CO3),
  `RecipeCutoutMaskKind` (`media`, and `image`, drawn since CO10b from the
  picture's one mask, CO-107),
  `RecipeCutoutMask` (`kind` and `media` required; `subject` lenient,
  `person` when absent, CO-101) and `RecipeCutout` (the recipe layer's
  `cutout`, `mask` required; `subjectCopy`, CO-51); `RecipeLayer.videoProps` passes no cutout — the recipe's is a draw
  instruction, not the clip's props. `VideoProps.swift` (`VideoProps`),
  `ClipSnapshot.swift` (`ClipSource` with its nested `CodingKeys`, `ClipSnapshot`,
  `TransitionSnapshot`) and `TrackSnapshot.swift` (`TrackSnapshot`) are pure moves out of
  `ProjectSnapshot.swift` (road map creator-jobs CJ0d, T11–T13). `ShapeProps.swift` (a pure
  move out of `ProjectSnapshot.swift`, grading L3) holds the shape group: `StrokeProps`,
  `GradientStop`, `Gradient` and `ShapeProps`. `GradeProps.swift` holds `ColorAdjust` (a pure move out of `ProjectSnapshot.swift`, grading-2 G2-0) beside grading's other value types. `ActionSnapshot.swift` (a pure move out of
  `ProjectSnapshot.swift`, B87) holds `ActionPatch`, `ActionSnapshot` and `ActionGraphicPatch` — an
  end's `graphic.props` and `kinds`, whose `dictionary` sends `props` only. `MediaSnapshot` (a pure move out of
  `ProjectSnapshot.swift`) carries a copy's or an ffmpeg conversion's `original`, and its `name` is
  the one display-name spelling: the original's name when one is recorded. **Its enums decode LENIENTLY**
  — a misspelt kind becomes the first case, a `T??` field a clear — which is
  why a caller-authored object is never decoded through them (below). The
  one exception is `ClipSource`: an unknown `source.kind` THROWS, and
  `ReelProject.snapshot` then falls back to `.empty`, so the WHOLE project
  draws empty with no error. A new source kind in the core is therefore a
  `ClipSource` case in the same phase (road map 10's G2a added `graphic`): no
  agent handler reads a caller-authored OBJECT at all. A scalar enum
  argument is a different thing and several handlers still parse one by name
  (`enumArg` for `add_zoom_action`'s `fit` or an action's `curve`,
  `set_transition`'s `kind` by hand): the
  core refuses those too, and what this rule forbids is decoding a caller's
  object through a lenient type.
  `MotionProps.dictionary` always writes all three keys, `NSNull` for a nil
  slot, because a core patch of `motion` deep-merges — it is the
  APP's writer saying all three slots, not a replace rule, and it is the only
  edge that writes a whole motion. `MotionEdge` also supplies nonpersisted
  zero-duration activity and inactive display/menu titles (E2-27).
  `TextProps.swift` is the text group and `RecipeReveal` (with format version
  9's `textCase` / `words` / `wordStyle`, the recipe's `word` / `wordPop` and,
  since format version 12, `wordGlide` / `wordFill` / `wordDim`), a pure move
  out of `ProjectSnapshot.swift` because a stored property cannot be added
  from an extension. `RecipeReveal` reads and writes its OWN keys — siblings of
  `hash` and `text` in the `text` source — through `init(siblingsOf:)` and
  `encodeSiblings(to:)`, so a new recipe key costs `FrameRecipe.swift`
  nothing; a key spelled other than the snake-case converter spells it
  decodes silently to that key's default (the amount to 1, the rest to nil).
  `ProjectSnapshot+Graphic.swift` mirrors
  `model_graphic.rs`'s `GraphicProps` as `GraphicSnapshot` (`in` is
  `sourceIn`) and `GraphicPropValue` (string, number, bool; anything else
  `.null`), decoded into `ClipSnapshot.graphic`; `props` keys keep the
  module's own spelling (snake-case conversion does not reach a dictionary's
  keys). `WordProps.swift` mirrors `model_words.rs`
  (`TextCase`, `TextWord`, `WordMode`, `ActivePill`, `WordStyle`)
  — `WordStyle.dictionary` writes ALL eight keys (`active_fill` and `pause_dim` since format version 12; `ActivePill.dictionary` writes `glide`), `NSNull` for a nil slot,
  `MotionProps.dictionary`'s rule, because the core deep-merges
  `word_style` — and holds
  what the renderer and the inspector share: `laidContent` (`case` applied —
  every layout and string index is in ITS UTF-16 space, never `content`'s),
  `tokenCount`, `isUntimedPage`, `TextPatch.contentEdit` and
  `InspectorBinding.contentOps` / `ops(textContent:)` — the Content write,
  decided PER CLIP: `words: []` beside the content in one `set_text` only for
  base clips whose count changed, and never `words` in an action end (W-2,
  W-6). It lives there, not in `InspectorPane.swift`, for the size rule.

**The document.**
- `ProjectDocument.swift` (+`DisplayStem`, +`Recording`, +`SelectedAction`, +`Import`, +`Graphics`, +`GraphicFiles`, +`UndoGroup`, +`CacheSaves`, +`Alerts`, +`Reverse`, +`Derived`)
  — NSDocument, `.framejob` package read/write, and the single mutation
  point (see Undo); `applyEdit`'s `.refused` arm beeps and then posts
  `projectDocumentDidRefuse` with the `ReelRefusal` (spec §11 CI-10), which
  the editor forwards to the inspector's refusal strip. Holds the SIX pieces of view state nothing persists —
  playhead, clip selection, in/out range, `selectedMedia`, `nestPath` and
  `selectedAction` — re-clamped by `clampViewState` in that order with the
  scope FIRST, since the selection clamp measures against whatever
  container the scope left. `selectedAction` (spec §11 CI-1) is nil or one
  action of the SINGLE selected clip; `+SelectedAction` holds its queries,
  its one deliberate writer `selectAction(_:)` (which stores nil for an id
  that is not `singleSelectedClip`'s) and the ENTRY rule
  `syncSelectedAction()`, run from `playhead`'s and `selection`'s `didSet`
  against `lastInsideAction`. The clamp re-reads `lastInsideAction` BEFORE
  its last line writes the playhead, so an edit, undo or redo under a
  stationary playhead never enters a span — keep those two lines above
  that write. `nestPath` is a
  PATH of (nest, clip) steps, not a nest id, because two clips can show one
  nest at two starts; `editedProject` is a STORED, memoised `rc_project_scoped`
  handle, and `project` still means the parent for save, export and
  consolidate. A range is cleared on every scope change: a pair of ticks means
  one thing inside a nest and another to an export. `+UndoGroup`:
  `inUndoGroupIfRegistered` runs a body with an undo group pending, and
  `registerUndo(restoring:actionName:)`'s first statement
  (`openPendingUndoGroup()`) opens it at the body's first registration, at the
  body's level and never while undoing or redoing; a body that registers
  nothing leaves undo and redo untouched (#167); `registerUndo` stays the one
  registrar. `applyEdit(_:_:amending:)` (#272) undoes the step that ended at
  `step` before committing, when `project` is still that handle, so a strip's
  off-knob double-click is one step. `cacheDirectory` calls `packageContentsDidChangeOnDisk()` when it
  creates `cache/` — only if the package's date, read through a fresh `URL`
  before the create, is still `fileModificationDate`, so an outside change made before it is not absorbed — and that method re-reads the date through a fresh
  `URL`, because `fileURL` still holds the date it cached at open (#138).
  `+CacheSaves` is the `save(to:ofType:for:completionHandler:)` override

**Frozen files.** `EditorViewController.swift`, `TimelineView.swift`,
`PreviewCanvasView.swift`, `AgentServer.swift` are **frozen at current
size**: anything adding more than ~50 lines goes in an extension file
(`EditorViewController+<Feature>.swift`, `TimelineView+<Feature>.swift`,
`AgentServer+<Feature>.swift`) or a new `…SheetController`, and the frozen
file keeps only the wiring — a stored property, a closure assignment, a
validator arm, a draw call. The pieces extension files build on are therefore
internal, not private. Pitfalls: a selector declared `@objc` on an extension
needs NO forward in the frozen file (a second declaration is an error); a
command whose body sits at the foot of a non-extension feature file carries
its validator arm there too, or the item falls through to the closing
`return true`; `handleEditorCharacter`'s bare-key `switch` matches in SOURCE
order, so a bare `case "x"` goes BELOW any modified `case "x" where …`; and
`handleEditorKey` refuses while a sheet is attached, because a sheet is
window-modal and the preview panel's forwarded keys would otherwise reach
the key map behind it.

**Frozen files.** `EditorViewController.swift`, `TimelineView.swift`,
`PreviewCanvasView.swift`, `AgentServer.swift` are **frozen at current
size**: anything adding more than ~50 lines goes in an extension file
(`EditorViewController+<Feature>.swift`, `TimelineView+<Feature>.swift`,
`AgentServer+<Feature>.swift`) or a new `…SheetController`, and the frozen
file keeps only the wiring — a stored property, a closure assignment, a
validator arm, a draw call. The pieces extension files build on are therefore
internal, not private. Pitfalls: a selector declared `@objc` on an extension
needs NO forward in the frozen file (a second declaration is an error); a
command whose body sits at the foot of a non-extension feature file carries
its validator arm there too, or the item falls through to the closing
`return true`; `handleEditorCharacter`'s bare-key `switch` matches in SOURCE
order, so a bare `case "x"` goes BELOW any modified `case "x" where …`; and
`handleEditorKey` refuses while a sheet is attached, because a sheet is
window-modal and the preview panel's forwarded keys would otherwise reach
the key map behind it.

# app/CLAUDE.md — Swift app rules

Applies to everything under `app/`. Build/verification commands and the FFI
lockstep are in the root `CLAUDE.md`; the full design is
`designs/spec/` (§3–4 the UI, §7.4–7.8 the platform side; its `README.md` is
the index). The
long form of each entry below — why each file is the shape it is, and the
traps its history turned up — is `designs/adr/app-file-history.md` (the
full history, every size toll and measurement, is archived; see its
"Original" line); this file is what governs a file now. Files
are listed by family; a file with a header comment of its own carries its
detail there.

## File map

**The core's edge.**
- `ReelCore.swift` — with its `ReelCore+<Area>.swift` files, the only files
  that call `rc_*` (spec §11 CJ-8 (l)); a new wrapper goes in the file of its
  area. `ReelCore.swift` holds `ReelProject`
  (handle + lazily decoded `ProjectSnapshot`; `json`, `snapshot` and
  `planJSON` are memoised PER HANDLE, so keep handles rather than minting
  them; so is `sourceMap(_:)`, `rc_project_source_map` decoded and checked
  once per handle and clip, SR-20), timecode, snapping (export presets/sizes/settings are
  `ExportValues.swift`'s, a pure move, HDR H-1), `ReelSpeed.limits` (the
  core's speed range and audio ceiling, typed as `SpeedLimits` in
  `CoreValues.swift` — no Swift file types a speed bound), `ReelColor` (`rc_normalise_color`, G-25) and `ReelAgentSocket` (below);
  `ReelCore+MediaFiles.swift` holds the media files the core reads or writes —
  `ReelContainer` (`rc_container_*`, a WebM/Matroska file's index, #216-R), `ReelCube`,
  `ReelHDR10` (`rc_hdr10_peak`, spec §11 HD-6; `av1Peak`, `rc_hdr10_av1_peak`, HD-18;
  `stillPeak`, `rc_hdr10_still_peak`, HD-20), `ReelAV1` and `ReelWebM` (`rc_webm_*`, the
  `av1_webm` writer, spec §11 CX-15) — `ReelCore+Cursor.swift` holds `ReelCursor`
  (`rc_cursor_open`, `rc_cursor_free`: a cursor file's open, which is its check, spec
  §11 CU-9, CU-15; road map creator-jobs CU1a; and `query`, `rc_cursor_query`'s one
  JSON request, CU2, spec §11 CU-25, and the static `query(_:tracks:project:)`, the
  same call over n tracks with a project (`plan_zooms`, CU-70)) — `ReelCore+Framing.swift`
  holds `SpeakerMatch` and `ReelProject.speakerMatch` (`rc_project_speaker_match`, road map
  creator-jobs VR6b, spec §11 VR-65: the face-to-microphone match Make Vertical's sheet
  confirms) — and `ReelCore+Graphics.swift` the graphics engine's
  wrappers (below), with `ReelGraphicPackage` (`rc_graphic_package_write`, G-46; `read`,
  `rc_graphic_package_read`, G-47), `GraphicLibrary.usage()` (`rc_graphic_library_usage`)
  and `GraphicLibrary.imageCache(limit:)` (`rc_graphic_image_cache`, G-39) — both pure moves
  out of `ReelCore.swift` (road map creator-jobs CJ0d, T15); `ReelCoreError`, `Fps.ffiPair` and `ReelTime`'s
  seconds conversions are `CoreValues.swift`'s (G6 phase 5's toll T2 and speed ramps SR4-0,
  pure moves); the typed patches are `TypedPatches.swift`'s (`VideoPatch`,
  `AudioPatch`, `ClipPatch`, the `ActionPatch` extension; a pure move, B73),
  `TextPatch` (with `case`, `words` and `word_style`) is `TextPatch.swift`'s,
  moved out so it could grow, and `ShapePatch` `ShapePatch.swift`'s (a pure
  move, the toll for `ReelColor`). `VideoPatch.color` is a sparse `ColorPatch`
  (`GradeProps.swift`, which holds `ColorAdjust` (moved out of
  `ProjectSnapshot.swift`, grading-2 G2-0) with its neutrality helpers, and
  `LayerUniforms.apply(tone:)`, and the wheels' `ColorWheel`, `ColorWheels`,
  `ColorWheelPatch`, `ColorWheelsPatch`, `ColorWheelKind` and
  `LayerUniforms.apply(wheels:)` (GR-11)); `VideoPatch.curves` is
  `CurveProps.swift`'s `ColorCurvesPatch`, beside `CurvePoint`,
  `CurveDomain`, `CurveChannel`, `CurveBlend` (a channel blended inside an
  action, spec §11 GR-34; `ColorCurves.blends`, never encoded), `ColorCurves` and
  `LayerUniforms.apply(curves:)` (GR-12, the hue curves GR-32; a
  pure move out of `GradeProps.swift`, grading-4 T4-0); `VideoPatch.qualifier` is

  `blur`, `blursSelection` and `selectionSigma`, GR-35), `QualifierUniforms`

  (GR-13), so a row writes
  only its own key to every selected clip. `word_style` has ONE
  app-side writer, `CaptionLayout.place` (W-10). `ReelAgentSocket` (road map
  14's MC2) wraps `rc_agent_socket_start` / `_release`: `start` throws the
  core's sentence, `release` is the quit's unlink-if-still-ours with no join;
  `answer(_:)` hands the tool callback's answer back through
  `rc_agent_string_create` (CJ0d's T15c), a plain static because the trampoline
  runs on the core's server thread, so `AgentServer.swift` names no `rc_*`.
  The `dictionary` extensions on the property types are
  `OpDictionaries.swift`'s (below).
  The graphics engine's wrappers are `ReelCore+Graphics.swift`'s: `GraphicLibrary` (`addFont`,

  rasterize or `families()`) and
  `GraphicModule` (`compile`, `describeJSON`, `svg`; it holds its library

  and `.of(_:)`, the one spelling of a diagnostic made from a message, a

  clean-up batch 2), `ReelCoreError` and `Fps.ffiPair` (G6 phase 5's toll), and

**Frozen files.** `EditorViewController.swift`, `TimelineView.swift`,
`PreviewCanvasView.swift`, `AgentServer.swift` are **frozen at current
size**: anything adding more than ~50 lines goes in an extension file
(`EditorViewController+<Feature>.swift`, `TimelineView+<Feature>.swift`,
`AgentServer+<Feature>.swift`) or a new `…SheetController`, and the frozen
file keeps only the wiring — a stored property, a closure assignment, a
validator arm, a draw call. The pieces extension files build on are therefore
internal, not private. Pitfalls: a selector declared `@objc` on an extension
needs NO forward in the frozen file (a second declaration is an error); a
command whose body sits at the foot of a non-extension feature file carries
its validator arm there too, or the item falls through to the closing
`return true`; `handleEditorCharacter`'s bare-key `switch` matches in SOURCE
order, so a bare `case "x"` goes BELOW any modified `case "x" where …`; and
`handleEditorKey` refuses while a sheet is attached, because a sheet is
window-modal and the preview panel's forwarded keys would otherwise reach
the key map behind it.

docs/guide/editing.md:22:Drag a file's row from the Media tab onto a track. What the drop does depends on the modifier keys you hold **when you release**:
docs/guide/editing.md:26:| No modifier | Places the whole file as a clip at the drop point. Nothing else moves. The drop is refused if the clip would overlap its neighbours in a way the overlap rule forbids. | Add Clip |
docs/guide/editing.md:27:| ⌥ | **Insert.** Splits the clip under the drop point on that track, pushes everything on every unlocked track later by the file's length, then places the file in the gap. Only the destination track is cut. Clips on other tracks that span the drop point stay where they are, uncut; only clips that start at or after it move later. The exception is a detached sound linked to a clip that is cut: it is cut at the same point, so the pair stays in step. | Insert |
docs/guide/editing.md:28:| ⇧⌥ | **Overwrite.** Clears the file's length from the drop point on that track alone, cutting at both ends and removing what lies between, then places the file. Nothing moves and no other track is touched, except that a detached sound linked to a clip that is cut is cut at the same points; its piece under the new file stays, no longer linked. | Overwrite |
docs/guide/editing.md:42:- **Onto a new track:** drop above the top lane to make a new front track, or below the bottom lane to make a new back track.
docs/guide/editing.md:44:- **Refused drops spring back.** If the drop breaks the overlap rule (see [Limits](#limits)), the clip animates back to where it was and nothing changes. While you drag, positions the project refuses are skipped, and the clip stays at the last allowed position.
docs/guide/editing.md:45:- **Overlaps make transitions.** A clip dropped so it overlaps the clip before it on the same track gets a Cross Dissolve over the overlap, unless it already has a transition. Clips never push each other out of the way. Other edits do the same; see [Overlaps make transitions](#overlaps-make-transitions).
docs/guide/editing.md:68:Hold ⌥ while you drag a media clip's **end** edge to stretch it instead. The clip's speed changes so that the same content fills the new length (undo name "Rate Stretch"). ⌥ on the start edge does an ordinary trim. If a stretch would take the clip above the speed where its sound is dropped, the app asks first. Speeds and their limits are covered in [Speed](speed.md).
docs/guide/editing.md:139:**Inserting time** opens empty room instead. Every clip on an unlocked track that starts at or after a point moves later by a length, and so does every marker at or after it. Clips that span the point stay put, so nothing is cut (split first if you want the room inside a clip). No menu item or gesture does this on its own. ⌥-drop insert and Freeze Frame both use it as part of their edit, and agents can call it directly.
docs/guide/editing.md:259:When a drag snaps, a vertical guide line across the timeline marks the point it snapped to. A media row dropped on a lane lands on the nearest frame at the pointer and doesn't snap to edges.
docs/guide/editing.md:281:During a drag, positions the project refuses are skipped and the clip waits at the last allowed position. Only the drop counts.
docs/guide/editing.md:321:| ⌥-drop / ⇧⌥-drop a media row | Insert / Overwrite at the drop |

82	Some things belong to the project, not to the nest you have open. They still work, and they change the whole project.
83	
84	- **Media:** the Media tab lists the project's media. Adding, relinking or removing a file works as usual. Dropping a file from Finder onto a nest's timeline adds it to the project and puts its clip in the nest, as one undo step.
85	- **The Document tab:** it shows the project's settings. Changing the project's size doesn't change the nest's size, which is [fixed](/editing/nests/).

50	3. Press <kbd>⌘G</kbd>. Those clips become a new nest, which shares nothing with the first.
51	
52	</Steps>
53	
54	Un-nesting drops the copy's own position, scale, opacity, fades and volume, so set those again on the new nest clip. The new nest also takes the project's current size, which may differ from the original's. Un-nesting gives back everything in the nest, so a [trim](#trim-a-nest-clip) on the copy is gone too.
55	
56	:::caution[Copy and Paste don't work on a nest clip]
57	**Edit ▸ Copy** leaves the nest itself behind, so **Edit ▸ Paste** shows an alert saying the pasted clip shows a nest "which the payload does not carry", and pastes nothing. That's true of any selection with a nest clip in it, in this project or another one.
58	
59	**Edit ▸ Cut** still removes the clip, so after a failed paste, press <kbd>⌘Z</kbd> until it's back.
60	:::
61	
62	## Trim a nest clip
63	
64	Trimming a nest clip changes how much of the nest plays. It never cuts anything out of the nest. The clip always plays from the nest's first frame for as long as the clip lasts, which makes its two edges behave differently from a media clip's:
65	
66	| Drag | What happens |
67	| --- | --- |
68	| The end edge in | The tail of the nest is hidden. |
69	| The end edge out | More of the nest plays. Past the end of the contents, the clip shows nothing. The contents set no limit on how far you can drag. |
70	| The start edge later | The clip starts later and the whole nest moves later with it. The opening still plays, and the tail is what gets hidden. |
71	| The start edge earlier | The nest moves earlier with it, and more of the tail plays. |
72	
73	So you can't hide a nest's opening with a trim. To do that, [open the nest](/editing/inside-a-nest/) and edit inside it, which changes every clip showing the nest.
74	
75	**Clip ▸ Un-nest** (<kbd>⇧⌘G</kbd>) gives back everything, however short the clip was trimmed. What was hidden returns at the nest clip's start plus its own time, and a clip that would then collide with what's after it goes on a new track in front.
76	
77	## With an agent
78	
79	An agent can make the independent copy in one step. `paste` copies a nest when its payload carries the nest as well as the clip, with every level inside it, and gives the copy nothing in common with the original. See [Tools: copying and nesting](/mcp/tools-copy-and-nest/).

# CLAUDE.md — the documentation site

The public user documentation: Astro with Starlight, one page per feature or tight family of
features. `pnpm` manages it, and `engines` in `package.json` sets the Node it needs. `README.md` has
the commands.

## Where things are

```
astro.config.mjs        Starlight's settings: title, logo, fonts, theme, plugins
sidebar.mjs             every page's place in the navigation, in order
src/content/docs/       the pages: <section>/<page>.mdx
src/data/features.json  THE FEATURE LIST: what /features/ renders and what the proof reads
src/components/         AtAGlance (a page's facts), Shot (a screen in both looks),
                        FeatureIndex (the filterable list)
src/assets/screens/     WebP captures, written only by scripts/import-screens.mjs
src/styles/             the brand: the mark's inks, the app's faces, square chrome
```

## The rule that matters

**Every claim is written from the code.** A label, a default, a range, a shortcut, a limit or a
refusal is checked against `app/Sources/`, `core/src/`, `graphic/` or `mcp-proxy/` before it is
written, and the code wins over `docs/guide/`, a spec or an ADR. Never write what a feature
probably does. If the code cannot settle it, leave it out.

Nothing dev-only, deferred or unbuilt is documented. That excludes the dev tools (`snapshot_ui`,
`perform_menu_item`, `cancel_sheet`, `select_inspector_tab`, `play_preview`, `graphic_memory`,
`loudness_meter`, `land_recording`, `analysis_job`, `transcript_view`, `playback_rebuilds`,
`assistant_send`, `assistant_answer`) and every `-RCDev` launch default.

## Who reads this

Someone editing a video, who has never read this repository. They want to know what a thing does,
how to do it, and what will stop them. They do not care how it is built.

So a page never mentions: spec or decision IDs (`AU-12`, `§11`), road maps, phases, issue numbers,
source file or type names, `rc_*` exports, format version numbers, proofs, tests, or the history
of a feature. Internal words get translated: "refused" becomes what the user sees ("Frame Job
won't do this while…"), "the core" and "the op" disappear. A tool name is the one exception: the
MCP pages and `tools=` in `AtAGlance` name agent tools, because those are the product's interface.

## Voice

- Plain, direct and second person. Say what it does, then how. Short sentences.
- Open with what the feature is for, in a sentence or two, before any steps.
- British spelling in prose, as `docs/guide/` does (colour, centre, grey, normalise), and the
  app's exact spelling for its own labels (the **Color** tab, **Normalize**).
- Contractions are fine. No marketing: never "powerful", "seamless", "effortless", "robust",
  "simply", "just", "easily", "unleash", "supercharge".
- Prefer a full stop or a comma to an em dash.
- State defaults, ranges and limits as numbers. Say what happens at the edges, because that is
  what a reader comes to a reference for.
- No filler sections. A page with nothing to say under a heading doesn't have that heading.

## Page shape

```mdx
---
title: Markers
description: One sentence, what this page helps you do. Search results show it.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

What the feature is for, in a sentence or two.

<AtAGlance menu="Mark ▸ Add Marker" keys="M" tools="add_marker" />

<Shot name="04-editor.window" alt="What the picture shows, for someone who can't see it." />

## Add a marker

<Steps>

1. Move the playhead to the moment.
2. Press <kbd>M</kbd>.

</Steps>

## Options

| Control | What it does | Default |
| ------- | ------------ | ------- |

## Good to know

Limits, edge cases and what stops it, in plain words.

## Related

- [Snapping](/timeline/snapping/)
```

Every section is optional except the opening. Order the task sections as a reader needs them.

- **Headings** start at `##`, are sentence case, and name the job: "Add a marker", not "Adding".
  A feature in `src/data/features.json` with an `anchor` needs a heading that makes that anchor.
- **Menus** are bold with `▸`, spelled as the app spells them: **Clip ▸ Split**.
- **Keys** use the app's symbols in `<kbd>`: <kbd>⌘T</kbd>. Inside `AtAGlance`, pass the string.
- **Controls** are bold where they appear in a step: choose **Save**.
- **Links** are root-absolute with a trailing slash: `/timeline/markers/#add-a-marker`. The build
  fails on a link or anchor that does not exist.
- **Asides** are for what a reader must not miss, not for decoration: `:::note`, `:::tip`,
  `:::caution`, `:::danger`.
- **Screens** come from `src/assets/screens/`. A `name` is the file name without its look and
  extension. Use a screen only when it shows what the page is about, not when the thing is out
  of frame, and give it real alt text.

## MDX traps

MDX is JSX. In prose, `{`, `}` and `<` start code. Put anything like `{x}`, `<1 s` or `a<b` in a
code span, or write it out ("under 1 s"). `<kbd>` and every component must close. A line starting
with `import` or `export` is code. Leave a blank line after an opening component tag and before
its closing tag, or the Markdown inside won't render.

## Checking a page

```sh
node docs/site/scripts/check-pages.mjs <page.mdx>…        # parses, imports, links, captures
python3 tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py --pages <page.mdx>…  # internal words, local paths
pnpm build                                                # in docs/site: the last word
```

## Screens

The captures come from the screen catalog (`designs/screens/`, `tools/proof/screens.py`), so the
pictures are of the real app. To refresh them:

```sh
python3 tools/proof/screens.py --out <dir>                      # from the repository root
node docs/site/scripts/import-screens.mjs <dir> --used
```

**This site is public.** `import-screens.mjs` refuses a capture whose layout dump holds a local
path, and its `CROP` table is the only way past that, by cutting the region away. Settings needs
it: its MCP section prints the helper's full path. Never weaken the refusal.

## When the app changes

A user-visible change edits its page here as well as `docs/guide/`, and a new feature adds its row
to `src/data/features.json`. `tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py` runs in `make test` and fails on a
menu item or agent tool the site doesn't document, a feature whose page or anchor is missing, or a
page that names something internal.
